pedagogy.concept: The root BU expresses existence, being, and coming into state. When used with prefixes or specific morphological derivations, its fundamental sense of 'being' shifts to actions such as becoming, arising, or causing to be.

meanings.English: To hold, to support, to maintain, to nourish
meanings.Hindi: dharan karna, poshan karna, sahara dena

pedagogy.concept: The root quDA\ Y means holding, supporting, or nourishing. Since it is primarily an Atmanepada root in its native form, it often emphasizes an action directed toward oneself or holding for one's own benefit. Through prefixes and derivative suffixes like the causative or desiderative, its sense expands to causing others to bear or sustaining actively.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat), atmanepada, third person singular
scenarios.meaning: To bear, sustain, or hold for oneself
scenarios.example_english: The mother holds the son on her chest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic) stem with parasmaipada endings
scenarios.meaning: To cause to bear, to support, or to maintain
scenarios.example_english: The king maintains his subjects.

meanings.English: To purify, to wash, to nourish, to feed
meanings.Kannada: Shuchi madu, pooshisu, benne, svachchha golisu
meanings.Hindi: Shuddh karna, poshan karna, safai karna
meanings.Bengali: Parishkar kora, poshon kora, shuddho kora
meanings.Chinese: Qingjie, xi di, yang yu, zi yang

pedagogy.concept: The root nijir primarily expresses the dual ideas of cleaning/purifying and nourishing/sustaining. Depending on the voice and affixes, its focus can shift between physical cleansing and internal or supportive care.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat), 3rd person singular, Atmanepada, root form with reduplication.
scenarios.meaning: Cleanses or purifies oneself.
scenarios.example_english: The sage purifies his body with water.

meanings.English: To separate, to divide, to distinguish
meanings.Hindi: alag karna, vibhajit karna, prithak karna
meanings.Bengali: alada kara, vibhakta kara, prithak kara

pedagogy.concept: The root vi-ji (in the sense of separation or dispersion) typically takes ātmanepada endings when emphasizing the reflexive or natural process of separating or branching out.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Atmanepada present tense
scenarios.meaning: To separate or branch out independently
scenarios.example_english: The tree separates its branches.

meanings.English: To pervade, to spread, to encompass, to extend

pedagogy.concept: The root viṣ (to pervade or extend) in the third gaṇa typically expresses the action of spreading or encompassing throughout a space.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Perfect tense (liṣ), third person singular
scenarios.meaning: Has pervaded or encompassed completely
scenarios.example_english: Fire has pervaded everything.

meanings.English: to flow, to drip, to shine, to radiate
meanings.Chinese: liu dong, di luo, fa guang

pedagogy.concept: The root Gf primarily denotes flowing or dripping liquids as well as shining or radiating light. Through specific derivational suffixes and prefixes, its sense shifts between passive dripping, active pouring, and causative actions.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: By reduplication and shifting to parasmaipada in the third person singular present
scenarios.meaning: To sprinkle or moisten actively
scenarios.example_english: He sprinkles clarified butter onto the fire.

meanings.English: To take by force, to seize, to overpower
meanings.Tamil: valiyil edu, pidithu kol, akkaram seyyi
meanings.French: prendre par la force, s'emparer, saisir

pedagogy.concept: The root hf expresses taking or seizing, specifically with force or mastery (prasahyakaraṇe). When used with various prepositions (upasargas), its meaning shifts dramatically from violent seizure to bringing, offering, or carrying away.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the upasarga pari to the root
scenarios.meaning: To avoid, to reject, or to abandon
scenarios.example_english: A wise person should avoid wicked company.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the upasarga ā to the root
scenarios.meaning: To bring, to fetch, or to gather
scenarios.example_english: The sage brings fuel wood from the forest.

meanings.English: To go, to move, to reach, to attain

pedagogy.concept: The root f (f) primarily means to go or move. In its reduplicated form in the third gaṇa, it often emphasizes habitual or intensive motion towards a goal.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Reduplication and present stem formation in the third gaṇa
scenarios.meaning: To bear, to carry, or to move forward continuously
scenarios.example_english: Fire bears or sustains the sun.

meanings.English: To go, to move, to flow, to run

pedagogy.concept: The root sf means to go or to move. As a tudadi or curadi verb, its meaning can extend to flowing or releasing, and causative forms emphasize setting something in motion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense active voice with the tudadi gaṇa vikaraṇa
scenarios.meaning: To move or to flow
scenarios.example_english: Water flows along the riverbank.

meanings.English: To scold, to revile, to shine, to glow
meanings.Bengali: tartsana kara, ninda kara, alokita haoa, chamakano
meanings.Chinese: chi ze, ze bei, fa guang, zhao yao

pedagogy.concept: The root Basa~ covers two distinct semantic fields: harsh verbal action (scolding or revoking) and physical illumination (shining or blazing). These senses remain consistent across primary derivations, though prefixes can specialize the context.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic) affix added to the root with vrddhi of the vowel
scenarios.meaning: To cause to shine or to cause to chide
scenarios.example_english: The sun illuminates the world.

meanings.English: To know, to understand, to perceive

pedagogy.concept: The root ki (to know) primarily takes Atmanepada endings as a tudadi or juhotadi root in various derived contexts, shifting its focus toward reflective understanding or the acquisition of knowledge for oneself.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Desiderative suffix (san) added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To wish to know, to investigate or treat medically
scenarios.example_english: The doctor treats the patient.

meanings.English: To know, to understand, to learn
meanings.Chinese: zhi dao, liao jie, ren shi

pedagogy.concept: The root kita~ primarily means to know or understand. When modified into causative or desiderative forms, it expresses the desire to know or the action of causing someone to know.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Desiderative suffix sa(pratyaya) added to the root with reduplication
scenarios.meaning: To wish to cure or treat (historically derived from wishing to know the remedy/disease)
scenarios.example_english: The doctor treats the patient.

meanings.English: To hasten, to run, to speed, to quicken
meanings.Kannada: vegavāgi nadedu, tvarisu, joru mādu, odu
meanings.Hindi: jaldi karna, tvarit karna, daudna, vega se chalna
meanings.Bengali: tvarā karā, druta calā, daudānō, bēge yāoyā
meanings.German: sich beeilen, eilen, rasen, schnell sein

pedagogy.concept: The root tura expresses rapid movement, haste, and quickening. In derived forms, its causative suffix induces an action of driving or urging others to move fast.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic) suffix added to the root with vowel strengthening
scenarios.meaning: to urge someone to hurry or to drive quickly
scenarios.example_english: The charioteer urges the horses to run fast

meanings.English: To sound, to make noise, to resound

pedagogy.concept: The root diza~ generally denotes the production of sound. Since this root has limited common derived nuances in standard classical literature, its primary usage remains focused on expressing sound.

meanings.English: To accumulate grain, to harvest corn, to collect wealth
meanings.Telugu: dhanyamu sampadinchuta, pantanu koruta, dhanamu koodhuta
meanings.Tamil: dhaniyam ceytal, aruvadai ceytal, porul serkka
meanings.Hindi: dhanya jama karna, fasal kaatna, dhan ikattha karna
meanings.Bengali: dhanya sanchay kara, fasal kata, sampad jama kara
meanings.French: amasser du grain, récolter, accumuler des richesses
meanings.Russian: sobirat zerno, zhat urozhay, nakaplivat bogatstvo
meanings.Chinese: shou huo liang shi, ji cun gu wu, ju ji cai fu

pedagogy.concept: The root Dana expresses the action connected with grain or wealth, specifically accumulating or harvesting corn. When modified through causative suffixes, it denotes causing someone to gather or produce grain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause someone to collect or harvest grain
scenarios.example_english: The master causes the servants to collect the grain.

meanings.English: To be born, to produce, to generate, to create

pedagogy.concept: The root 'jana~' primarily expresses the action of birth, origination, or coming into existence. In its causative form, it shifts from the basic intransitive sense of being born to the transitive sense of generating or bringing something into existence.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix (nic) applied to the root, shifting the intransitive sense to transitive.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to be born, to produce or generate.
scenarios.example_english: Rain produces plants.

meanings.English: To praise, to laud, to sing in praise
meanings.Hindi: Stuti karna, prashansa karna, gun gaan karna

pedagogy.concept: The root gā belongs to the third conjugation (juhotyādi-gaṇa) and primarily expresses the act of praising or singing hymns. As an Ātmanepada root, the focus of the praise often reflects back upon the agent or is performed in a dedicated, solemn manner.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat), third-person singular, ātmanepada
scenarios.meaning: He praises or sings a hymn of praise.
scenarios.example_english: The devotee praises the god.

meanings.English: To play, to gamble, to shine, to praise, to rejoice
meanings.Hindi: Khelna, juwa khelna, chamakna, stuti karna, prasanna hona
meanings.Bengali: Khela kara, jita, alokita hawa, stuti kara, ananda kara
meanings.German: Spielen, glänzen, loben, sich freuen, leuchten
meanings.French: Jouer, briller, louer, se réjouir, rayonner
meanings.Chinese: Wan, du bo, fa guang, zhan mei, gao xing

pedagogy.concept: The root divu has a remarkably wide semantic range covering play, victory, desire, shining, and motion. In causative and prefixed forms, these nuances shift to emphasize specific actions like causing delight or illuminating.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic pratyaya)
scenarios.meaning: To cause to play or to cause to shine
scenarios.example_english: The child causes the toy to play / shine.

meanings.English: To sew, to stitch, to thread, to string

pedagogy.concept: The root zivu means to sew or join with a thread, and its derivatives typically focus on the action of stitching or causing someone else to sew.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat), 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: He sews or stitches
scenarios.example_english: The tailor sews the cloth.

meanings.English: To flow, to dry up, to waste away

pedagogy.concept: The root srivu conveys the dual notions of moving or flowing and of diminishing or drying up. Derived forms can emphasize either the physical motion of flowing or the causative action of causing something to wither or dry up.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Imperfect tense (laṅ), parasmaipada, third person singular
scenarios.meaning: It flowed or it dried up
scenarios.example_english: The water flowed swiftly in the river.

meanings.English: To spit, to eject, to throw out

pedagogy.concept: The root zWivu~ generally conveys the action of spitting or ejecting something from the mouth. Through standard suffixes and prefixes, it can indicate the direction or intensity of the ejection.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the upasarga pra- to the present tense form
scenarios.meaning: To spit forward or expectorate actively
scenarios.example_english: You are spitting to the side.

meanings.English: To eat, to take, to not see

pedagogy.concept: This root covers distinct physical actions such as consuming food, grasping or taking something, and the absence of visibility. Because it is a specialized and less common root, it does not have widely differentiated voice nuances like parasmaipada versus ātmanepada shifts worth teaching through scenarios.

meanings.English: To crush, to destroy, to consume, to expel
meanings.Kannada: Nuchchunuru maDu, naSha madu, tinnu, hodarisu
meanings.Bengali: Pisha fela, dhwongso kora, khaoya, taran kora

pedagogy.concept: The root zRasu conveys the dual actions of consuming or crushing and casting away or expelling. Through the addition of causative suffixes or prepositions, the nuance shifts from a literal physical destruction to various metaphorical expressions of elimination.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the ṇic suffix to denote the causative action of compelling destruction or removal.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to crush or throw away
scenarios.example_english: He causes the bracelet to be crushed or discarded.

meanings.English: (uncertain)

pedagogy.concept: This root is quite rare and lacks common or attested derived-form nuances that are typically useful to teach for general Sanskrit learners.

meanings.English: To burn, to scorch, to consume with fire

pedagogy.concept: The root vyuza implies burning or scorching. In its causative form, it signifies causing an object to be consumed by fire or heat.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to burn or to set on fire
scenarios.example_english: The fire causes the wood to burn.

meanings.English: To burn, to scorch, to consume by fire

pedagogy.concept: The root pluza~ primarily conveys the action of burning or scorching. Through different grammatical processes like the causative, the action can be directed outward onto an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Adding the causative suffix -aya to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to burn or to set on fire
scenarios.example_english: The fire causes the wood to burn.

meanings.English: To dance, to leap, to gesture with limbs

pedagogy.concept: The root nftI~ primarily denotes physical movement or dancing. When modified into causative or desiderative forms, the sense shifts to causing someone else to dance or desiring to dance.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix -nic added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to dance, to make someone dance
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the pupil dance.

meanings.English: To tremble, to fear, to be agitated, to shudder

pedagogy.concept: The root trasI~ expresses fear, trembling, or agitation. In its causative form, it shifts from experiencing fear oneself to causing someone else to tremble or become terrified.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix -nic added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To terrify, to cause to tremble
scenarios.example_english: Having seen the lion, the deer quickly terrifies (others) or causes trembling.

meanings.English: To rot, to putrefy, to decay, to spoil

pedagogy.concept: The root kuTa~ primarily expresses the process of becoming foul or rotting. In its causative form, it indicates the action of causing something to rot or decompose.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix (nic) added to the root to indicate making something rot.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to rot or putrefy
scenarios.example_english: He causes the fruit to rot with frost.

meanings.English: To injure, to hurt, to harm, to destroy
meanings.Kannada: Himse māḍu, noヴィsu, gāya māḍu
meanings.Hindi: Hinsā karnā, chot denā, nukasān karnā
meanings.Bengali: Hiṁsā karā, āghāt karā, kṣati karā
meanings.French: Blesser, faire du mal, nuire, détruire
meanings.Chinese: 伤害, 毁坏, 侵害

pedagogy.concept: The root puTa~ conveys the primary sense of injury or violence. In derived forms such as the causative, the action of causing someone else to inflict harm or pain becomes prominent.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic) suffix added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to injure or to order to harm
scenarios.example_english: The master causes the servant to injure.

meanings.English: To cover, to wrap, to surround, to conceal
meanings.Chinese: bao guo, zhe gai, huan rao, yin cang

pedagogy.concept: The root guDa~ primarily means to cover, wrap, or enclose. When modified into causative or desiderative forms, the basic sense of enclosing or concealing is intensified or directed toward an action.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Adding the ṇic suffix to cause someone to cover or wrap an object.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to wrap or to cause to cover
scenarios.example_english: The mother causes the child to be wrapped with a cloth.

meanings.English: To throw, to cast, to hurl, to send

pedagogy.concept: The root kṣip generally means to throw or send. When used with different prefixes or causative forms, its sense can shift from a physical throwing to directing thoughts or inciting actions.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense basic form indicating physical action
scenarios.meaning: To throw or hurl an object.
scenarios.example_english: The boy throws a stone on the ground.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the upasarga 'ni'
scenarios.meaning: To place down, deposit, or put away.
scenarios.example_english: She puts down the book outside.

meanings.English: To bloom, to blossom, to flower

pedagogy.concept: The root puzpa expresses the natural action of blooming or opening up, which can be extended through causative forms to mean causing something else to flourish or blossom.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the ṇic suffix to the root to indicate making or causing an action to happen.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to bloom or to make something flourish.
scenarios.example_english: Spring causes the creepers to blossom.

meanings.English: To become wet, to be moist, to wet

pedagogy.concept: The root tima~ primarily conveys the sense of becoming wet or moist. Through causative derivation, it extends to the active action of wetting or moistening something else.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic) suffix added to the root to indicate causing someone or something else to become wet.
scenarios.meaning: To moisten, to make wet
scenarios.example_english: The water moistens the hand.

meanings.English: To become wet, to be moist, to get soaked

pedagogy.concept: The root tIma~ belongs to the fourth gaṇa and primarily expresses the process of becoming wet or moist. In causative constructions, it shifts from an intransitive state of getting wet to the transitive action of wetting or moistening something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to form the causative stem, expressing the agent causing the action.
scenarios.meaning: To moisten or make something wet
scenarios.example_english: The gardener makes the creeper moist.

meanings.English: To become wet, to become moist, to dampen

pedagogy.concept: The root zwima~ expresses the process of becoming wet or moist. In its causative form, it shifts from an intransitive state of becoming moist to actively moistening or making something wet.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to form the causative stem, meaning to cause to become wet.
scenarios.meaning: To moisten, to wet
scenarios.example_english: The rain causes the earth to become wet.

meanings.English: To become wet, to be moist, to grow damp

pedagogy.concept: The root zwIma~ primarily expresses the physical state of becoming wet or moist. Through causative formation, it shifts from describing a natural state to actively causing an object to become wet.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix णिच् (ṇic) added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To moisten or wet something actively
scenarios.example_english: The water moistens the ground.

meanings.English: To urge, to impel, to feel ashamed, to be bashful
meanings.Bengali: prerana kara, lajjita hawa, lajja paoya
meanings.German: antreiben, drängen, sich schämen, verlegen sein
meanings.Chinese: tui dong, cu cu, gan dao xiu kui, hai pa

pedagogy.concept: The root vrīḍ represents two distinct semantic threads: urging or impelling someone, and experiencing shame or bashfulness. In its basic forms, it conveys the feeling of shyness or modesty.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic) formation derived from the root.
scenarios.meaning: To cause someone to feel ashamed or to put someone to shame.
scenarios.example_english: He puts him to shame with his work.

meanings.English: To go, to move, to seek, to desire

pedagogy.concept: The root iza~ primarily means motion or going, but in common usage it frequently extends to seeking or desiring an object of motion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat) active in 4th gana
scenarios.meaning: To desire or wish for something
scenarios.example_english: The boy desires a fruit

meanings.English: To be able, to endure, to tolerate, to overcome
meanings.Bengali: saksham hawa, sahya kara, jay kara

pedagogy.concept: The root sah (listed as zah) primarily conveys the meaning of enduring, bearing, or having the power to accomplish something. Through standard morphological additions, it can express completed action or causative force without changing its fundamental sense of capacity and endurance.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Aorist tense, first-person singular
scenarios.meaning: I endured or I was able to bear
scenarios.example_english: I endured the sorrow.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative stem (nic)
scenarios.meaning: To cause to endure or to tolerate
scenarios.example_english: He causes that sorrow to be endured.

meanings.English: (uncertain)

pedagogy.concept: This is a rare root with uncertain attestation and specific lexical application, hence no complex derived nuances are broadly taught.

meanings.English: To grow old, to decay, to age, to waste away
meanings.Hindi: būḍhā honā, kṣīṇa honā, ghisanā, jarānā
meanings.Bengali: baḍe hōwā, kṣīṇa haoyā, khōẏā, kṣaẏa haoyā
meanings.Russian: staret', tchat' v zad, vukhadit', tustit'
meanings.Chinese: lao hua, shuai tui, xiao mo, sun hai

pedagogy.concept: The root jFz primarily denotes decay, aging, or loss of vigor with time. Through causative formation, it expresses the action of causing something to age, digest, or wear out.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, parasmaipada, 4th gaṇa
scenarios.meaning: To grow old or wear out naturally
scenarios.example_english: Time causes all beings to wear out.

meanings.English: To decay, to wither, to age, to diminish

pedagogy.concept: The root JFz belongs to the fourth gaṇa and primarily expresses the process of growing old, decaying, or losing vigor with time. Through causative and descriptive suffixes, the sense shifts towards causing decay or experiencing the gradual loss of youth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, parasmaipada, fourth gaṇa
scenarios.meaning: To decay or age naturally over time
scenarios.example_english: Everything decays with time.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative form (ṇic)
scenarios.meaning: To cause to decay, digest, or age someone
scenarios.example_english: Warm water digests the consumed food.

meanings.English: To generate, to bear, to produce, to give birth
meanings.Hindi: paida karnā, janm denā, utpanna karnā

pedagogy.concept: The root zUN primarily means to give birth or bring forth offspring. In causative formations, it extends to causing something to be produced or generated.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the ṇic suffix to form the causative stem
scenarios.meaning: To cause to give birth or to prompt generation
scenarios.example_english: The mother brings forth the child.

meanings.English: To pain, to afflict, to distress, to suffer
meanings.Hindi: dukh dena, klesh dena, pidit karna
meanings.Bengali: kashta deoya, byatha deoya, pidita kara

pedagogy.concept: The root dūṅ generally conveys the sense of causing pain or suffering. When used in causative forms or with specific upasargas, the nuance can shift from subjective suffering to actively inflicting distress upon others.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative or derived intensive/transitive usage denoting the action of causing pain
scenarios.meaning: To cause pain, to torment someone
scenarios.example_english: Sin torments a person.

meanings.English: To waste away, to decay, to perish, to wane
meanings.Kannada: Kshina vagu, nasha hondu, tarigu, kagu
meanings.Chinese: Xiao shou, shuai tui, jian shao

pedagogy.concept: The root dīȃN inherently expresses the gradual loss of substance, power, or volume. Through causative formations, it can also signify the active diminishing or destroying of something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Adding the causative suffix -aya to indicate making something waste away or cause to decay.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to waste away, to exhaust, to deplete
scenarios.example_english: He causes the wealth to dwindle away.

meanings.English: To fly, to soar, to move through the air
meanings.German: Fliegen, sich in der Luft bewegen
meanings.French: Voler, se deplacer dans les airs

pedagogy.concept: The root qIN primarily denotes flying or moving through the sky. By adding grammatical suffixes such as the causal, the sense shifts to causing something else to fly or soar.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Atmanepada ending indicating reflexive or dependent motion
scenarios.meaning: To fly along or move across the sky
scenarios.example_english: The bird flies in the sky.

meanings.English: To hold, to support, to disregard
meanings.Chinese: Zhi cheng, bao chi, shi luo

pedagogy.concept:
The root DI
 carries multiple divergent senses including supporting, taking, and showing disregard. Because it is exclusively Atmanepada, the action often reflects back upon the agent's mental stance or personal holding.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (laṭ), 3rd person singular, Atmanepada
scenarios.meaning: To hold or support for oneself
scenarios.example_english: The mother supports the child.

meanings.English: To injure, to hurt, to kill, to harm

pedagogy.concept: The root mīṅ primarily expresses the act of injuring or harming. Through standard grammatical transformations like the causative suffix, its sense shifts from the base action of experiencing or performing harm to actively causing harm to another.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the root to indicate causing someone else to perform or undergo the action.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to injure or to cause harm
scenarios.example_english: He causes the enemy to be injured.

meanings.English: To flow, to drip, to ooze
meanings.Chinese: liu dong, di luo, shen lou

pedagogy.concept: The root rī (rīṅ) primarily means to flow or to ooze. In its common causative form, it conveys the action of causing something to flow or drip.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic) affix added to the root to indicate causing an action
scenarios.meaning: To cause to flow or to make drip
scenarios.example_english: The sprinkler makes the water flow.

meanings.English: To cling, to adhere, to stick, to embrace

pedagogy.concept:
The root lI (li
̃N) in the fourth class (divādi) taking ātmanepada primarily expresses the sense of clinging, adhering, or dissolving into something. Through causative or descriptive formations, this sense of clinging or sticking can be directed transitively toward an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (laT), third person singular, ātmanepada
scenarios.meaning: Clings, adheres, or dissolves into
scenarios.example_english: Water clings in the mud

meanings.English: To choose, to select, to prefer
meanings.Bengali: Pachhondo kora, bachhai kora, bohron kora

pedagogy.concept: The root vrīN primarily expresses the act of choosing or selecting. In its standard ātmanepada forms, the action often emphasizes personal preference or benefiting oneself through the choice made.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, 3rd person singular, ātmanepada
scenarios.meaning: He chooses or selects for himself
scenarios.example_sanskrit: saḥ svayaṃ varam ātmanaḥ śreṣṭham vṛṇīte.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic) formation in the tenth gaṇa
scenarios.meaning: To cause to protect or to set free
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the spy to be protected.

meanings.English: To praise, to laud, to extol, to commend
meanings.Hindi: stuti karana, prashamsa karana, badhai dena

pedagogy.concept: The root Iqa~ (class 10) primarily means to praise or laud. In its causative and participial forms, it frequently emphasizes a formal, reverent act of adoration directed toward divine figures or respected teachers.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Past passive participle formed withta suffix
scenarios.meaning: Praised or adored

meanings.English: To injure, to hurt, to harm, to kill
meanings.Chinese: 伤害, 损害, 杀害

pedagogy.concept: The root jasu~ generally conveys the sense of harming or injuring. In causative formations, it expresses the action of causing someone to injure or cause harm to another.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nijanta) suffix ṇic added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to injure or harm

meanings.English: To gather, to assemble, to accumulate, to combine

pedagogy.concept: The root piqi~ primarily expresses the action of gathering, compiling, or accumulating things together. In causative and nominal formations, this sense often extends to forming compact groups, compressing materials, or synthesizing scattered elements into a unified whole.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Adding the causative suffix -aya to the 10th gaṇa root to denote causing an action of gathering or compacting.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to gather or to press together
scenarios.example_english: He causes the grasses to be gathered together.

meanings.English: To throw, to cast, to hurl, to project

pedagogy.concept: The root parTa~ primarily means to throw or cast. In its causative form, it shifts the focus to making or causing something to be thrown.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, 3rd person singular, parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: He throws or casts
scenarios.example_english: The boy throws the toy.

meanings.English: To anger, to be angry, to enrage
meanings.Hindi: krodh karna, gussa karna, rosh dikhana
meanings.French: se fâcher, être en colère, courroucer

pedagogy.concept: The root ruza~ primarily expresses the mental state of anger or wrath. In its base form, it denotes experiencing or showing anger, while derived forms like the causative highlight the act of provoking anger in others.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to the base root
scenarios.meaning: To cause someone to become angry or to provoke wrath
scenarios.example_english: The mother causes the naughty child to become angry.

meanings.English: To be angry, to enrage, to provoke, to display anger
meanings.Hindi: Krodhit hona, gussa karna, rosh dikhana
meanings.Bengali: Krodh kora, rāg kora, rosh prakash kora
meanings.German: Zornig sein, sich ärgern, wütend werden
meanings.French: Être en colère, se fâcher, s'irriter

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to the tenth gaṇa root to express causing another to do the action.
scenarios.meaning: To cause someone to become angry, to provoke wrath.
scenarios.example_english: He makes the pupil angry.

meanings.English: To throw, to cast, to hurl, to toss

pedagogy.concept: The root qipa~ generally means to throw or cast. In the causative form, it takes on the sense of causing something or someone to throw or direct an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of ṇic suffix to express causing an action
scenarios.meaning: To cause to throw or project
scenarios.example_english: The boy causes the ball to be thrown.

meanings.English: To raise, to elevate, to lift up, to exalt
meanings.Chinese: ti sheng, ju qi, zan mei

pedagogy.concept: The root zwupa~ primarily conveys the meaning of raising or exalting. In its derived forms such as the causative, the action of causing something to be raised or praised becomes prominent.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to the tenth gaṇa root to indicate the causative action.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to raise or to cause to praise.
scenarios.example_english: The other person caused the architect to elevate the structure.

meanings.English: To accumulate, to pile up, to heap, to raise high
meanings.Hindi: ekatra karna, dher lagana, uncha karna
meanings.Chinese: ji lei, dui ji, gao zhang

pedagogy.concept: The root zwUpa~ fundamentally means accumulation or raising something high. Through causative and prefixed derivations, it denotes the deliberate act of piling objects together or elevating structures.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: adding the nic suffix to form the causative stem
scenarios.meaning: to cause to heap or to pile up
scenarios.example_english: The laborer piles up the wood.

meanings.English: To collect, to gather, to pile up, to heap
meanings.Bengali: ekatra kara, sangraha kara, jama kara
meanings.Chinese: ju ji, ji xu, gou pei

pedagogy.concept: The root cita carries the core sense of gathering or piling up. In the tenth gaṇa, it often takes causative-like or denominative nuances focusing on deliberate arrangement and collection.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, parasmaipada, tenth gaṇa
scenarios.meaning: To gather or collect things systematically
scenarios.example_english: He gathers the firewood.

meanings.English: To bite, to sting, to gnaw

pedagogy.concept: The root daSi~ fundamentally expresses the action of biting or stinging. When modified into forms like the causative or desiderative, the nuance shifts to causing someone else to bite or wishing to bite.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to bite or sting
scenarios.example_english: The snake causes the deer to be bitten.

meanings.English: To see, to bite, to look, to perceive

pedagogy.concept: The root dasi has a dual sense encompassing both seeing and biting. Depending on the derivation and context, it shifts between visual perception and physical action.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, parasmaipada, third person singular
scenarios.meaning: He sees or he bites depending on the immediate context of observation or action.
scenarios.example_english: The boy, seeing the snake, looks closely at it.

meanings.English: To show, to bite, to see, to exhibit

pedagogy.concept: The root dasa carries dual semantic directions relating to seeing or showing, and biting or piercing. Through the causative and nominal derivations, these senses clearly branch into active exhibition and aggressive contact.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the ṇic suffix to convey causing someone to see or show something.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to see, to display, to exhibit
scenarios.example_english: The teacher shows the lesson to the student.

meanings.English: (uncertain)

meanings.English: To gather, to collect, to assemble, to accumulate

pedagogy.concept: The root qipa~ belongs to the tenth gaṇa and primarily expresses the action of gathering or collecting things together. In its causative and derived forms, it typically emphasizes the intentional act of causing items or beings to assemble.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat), parasmaipada, third person singular of the basic tenth gaṇa root
scenarios.meaning: Gathers or accumulates
scenarios.example_english: He gathers wealth.

meanings.English: To support a family, to maintain, to sustain
meanings.Hindi: Parivar ka palan karna, poshan karna, nirvah karna

pedagogy.concept: The root tatri~ in the tenth gaṇa specifically relates to the sustenance and support of a household or family. By adding causative or nominal suffixes, the scope of maintaining expands from domestic duty to general preservation.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (laṭ) third person singular in the tenth gaṇa

scenarios.example_english: He supports his own family.

meanings.English: To consult secretly, to whisper, to plot

meanings.Chinese: mi mi shang liang, qiao qiao hua

pedagogy.concept: The root matri~ primarily denotes private consultation, whispering, or plotting. In derived forms, its scope expands from simple secret speech to the formal state craft of political counsel and ministerial deliberation.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (laṭ), parasmaipada, third person singular from the 10th gaṇa curādi.
scenarios.meaning: He consults secretly or deliberates in private.
scenarios.example_english: The king consults secretly with his ministers.

meanings.English: To touch, to grasp, to contact, to unite

pedagogy.concept: The root spaSa~ generally means to touch, contact, or grasp. In its causative or derived forms, the action of touching or making contact can be directed toward causing perception or binding things together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic) added to the base root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to touch or to send spies (making contact with information)
scenarios.example_english: The king sends a spy into the village.

meanings.English: To threaten, to scold, to intimidate, to blame
meanings.Bengali: humki dewa, bhoy dekhano, tarsana, ghurani
meanings.Chinese: wei xie, kong he, ze bei, qian ze

pedagogy.concept: The root tarj means to threaten or scold. In its causative form or with common prefixes like ud- or prati-, the nuance shifts toward explicit provocation, shouting warnings, or challenging someone directly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat), parasmaipada, 3rd person singular

scenarios.example_english: The wicked boy threatens his master.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic) stem formation
scenarios.meaning: He causes to threaten or frightens
scenarios.example_english: The hunter causes terror to him who dwells in the forest.

meanings.English: To threaten, to chide, to scold, to revile

pedagogy.concept: The root Bartsa~ primarily expresses the action of threatening or scolding. In its causative and nominalized derivatives, the nuance shifts toward creating fear or expressing strong disapproval.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat), parasmaipada, 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: He threatens or scolds someone.
scenarios.example_english: The master threatens the wicked servant.

meanings.English: To torment, to harass, to afflict
meanings.Chinese: 折磨, 痛苦, 骚扰

pedagogy.concept: The root basta (ardane) primarily means to torment or afflict. In the causative form, it expresses the action of causing someone else to inflict pain or to harass another.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic) added to the root to denote causing another to torment
scenarios.meaning: To cause to torment or harass
scenarios.example_english: The master causes the servant to torment the laborer.

meanings.English: To torment, to afflict, to pain
meanings.Bengali: kashta deoya, jantrana deoya, pidan kara

pedagogy.concept: The root ganDa~ belongs to the tenth gaṇa and primarily conveys the sense of causing pain, tormenting, or afflicting. Through causative and derivative formations, this core action of affliction can be directed toward an object or expressed as a mutual state.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (laṭ) active form in the tenth gaṇa
scenarios.meaning: He torments or causes pain to someone
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person torments an innocent person.

meanings.English: To throw, to cast, to hurl

pedagogy.concept: The root kila~ generally expresses the action of throwing, casting, or hurling an object. In its causative form, it indicates compelling or causing someone else to throw or hurl.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic) present tense third person singular
scenarios.meaning: Causes to throw or hurl
scenarios.example_english: He causes the arrow to be hurled.

meanings.English: To throw, to cast, to hurl, to project

pedagogy.concept: The root pila carries the basic meaning of throwing or casting. In its standard causative or derived forms, it can express the action of causing something to be thrown or projecting an object towards a target.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the tenth gaṇa root to express making someone throw.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to throw or project
scenarios.example_english: He causes the horse to throw.

meanings.English: To injure, to hurt, to kill, to harm
meanings.Tamil: tiṅgu sey, thīṅgu viḷaivai, kol, varuththu
meanings.Hindi: hinsā karanā, chot pahunchānā, mārnā, nuksan pahunchānā

meanings.French: blesser, nuire, tuer, faire du mal

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the ṇic suffix to the root to signify causing someone else to injure or cause harm.
scenarios.meaning: To cause someone to injure or harm
scenarios.example_english: He causes harm to the enemy.

meanings.English: To injure, to hurt, to harm, to kill

pedagogy.concept: The root hizka~ belongs to the tenth conjugation (curādi-gaṇa) and inherently carries the meaning of injuring or causing harm. In its causative and derived forms, it typically emphasizes the act of causing pain or destruction to an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Yananta (intensive) formation

meanings.English: To weigh, to measure, to assess value

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present indicative (laṭ) third person singular in parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: He weighs or measures out

meanings.English: To desire, to long for, to wish, to crave

meanings.English: To contract, to shrink, to draw together, to close

pedagogy.concept: The root kURa~ primarily denotes physical contraction or shrinking. When used in different derived forms such as the causative, it expresses the deliberate action of causing something to contract or close.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative marker nic added to the root to denote making someone or something contract.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to contract or close

meanings.English: To fill, to fulfill, to complete, to satisfy

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, third-person singular, parasmaipada of the tenth class

meanings.English: To hope, to expect, to doubt, to fear

meanings.English: To praise, to flatter, to boast
meanings.Hindi: Prashamsa karna, tarif karna, stuti karna

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Adding the causative suffix -aya to the root

meanings.English: To worship, to adore, to honour

scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the disciple to worship the gods.

meanings.English: To deliberate, to doubt, to reflect, to surmise

meanings.English: To lift, to raise, to exert, to offer

scenarios.example_english: He investigates the matter.

meanings.English: To observe, to notice, to mark, to perceive

meanings.Bengali: lakshya kara, dekha, dhyan deya, bichar kara

meanings.English: To despise, to blame, to revile, to scorn

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the root to denote causing an action

meanings.English: To trickle, to drip, to ooze, to flow

meanings.English: To bind, to tie, to fasten, to empower

meanings.English: To gladden, to satisfy, to please

pedagogy.concept: The root rUkza in the tenth gaNa conveys the sense of roughness, harshness, or treating something with severity. Through causative and derivative formations, it describes the act of making an object or speech rough and harsh.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: 10th gaNa present tense active third-person singular
scenarios.meaning: He makes something rough or speaks harshly
scenarios.example_english: He makes his speech harsh.

meanings.English: To finish, to complete, to accomplish, to cross

pedagogy.concept: The root pAra in the tenth gaNa conveys the sense of bringing an action to completion or conclusion. Through causative suffixes or verbal prefixes, its basic meaning of finishing can be extended to crossing over to the other side or fulfilling a task.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, 3rd person singular in the 10th gaNa
scenarios.meaning: To finish, to complete or accomplish
scenarios.example_english: He completes all the work.

meanings.English: To finish, to complete, to accomplish, to conclude
meanings.Chinese: wan cheng, jie shu, tuo shan

pedagogy.concept: The root tIr belongs to the tenth gaṇa and primarily means to finish or complete an action. In its causative or derived forms, it emphasizes bringing an ongoing task or journey to its final destination or conclusion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: tenth gaṇa present indicative active
scenarios.meaning: completes, finishes, fulfills
scenarios.example_english: He completes his work.

meanings.English: To contact, to unite, to combine, to mix

pedagogy.concept: The root puwa generally denotes contact or bringing things together. When modified into causative or derived forms, the nuance shifts to causing an object to be combined, enclosed, or folded together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic) of the 10th gaṇa root puwa
scenarios.meaning: To cause to contact, to enclose, or to fold together
scenarios.example_english: He causes the leaf to be folded together with another leaf.

meanings.English: To loosen, to relax, to make slack, to soften
meanings.Kannada: saithilya madu, bigita kisu, sithila golisu
meanings.Hindi: dhila karna, sithila karna, shithilata lana

pedagogy.concept: The root katra belongs to the tenth gaṇa and carries the core sense of loosening, making slack, or causing relaxation (śaithilya). Through the addition of causative or nominal suffixes, it typically highlights the active process of slackening an object or a bond.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat), third person singular, parasmaipada of the tenth gaṇa root
scenarios.meaning: He/she/it loosens or relaxes something.
scenarios.example_english: He loosens the rope.

meanings.English: To loosen, to relax, to slacken

pedagogy.concept: The root karta~ denotes making loose or slack (shaithilya). In causative and derived forms, it typically emphasizes the action of causing something to become loose, untied, or relaxed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the ṇic suffix to express causing an action or state
scenarios.meaning: To cause to loosen or slacken
scenarios.example_english: He loosens the rope.

meanings.English: to see, to look at, to observe

pedagogy.concept: The root valka in the tenth conjugation expresses the act of seeing or observing. When causative suffixes or prepositions are applied, the nuance shifts toward causing someone to see or inspecting closely.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, third-person singular in the tenth conjugation
scenarios.meaning: To look at or to observe
scenarios.example_english: He looks at the forest.

meanings.English: To variegate, to paint, to picture, to make motley
meanings.Chinese: hua hua, miao hui, cai hui

pedagogy.concept: The root citra in the tenth conjugation expresses the act of making something variegated, adorned, or vividly pictured. Through the causative-like nature of the tenth gaṇa, the base meaning shifts towards creative representation or detailed description.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat), third person singular, parasmaipada of the tenth gaṇa
scenarios.meaning: He paints or variegates
scenarios.example_english: The painter decorates the wall.

meanings.English: To strike, to hit, to collide
meanings.Chinese: da ji, peng zhuang, chong ji

pedagogy.concept: The root ansa in the tenth conjugation expresses the action of striking or colliding. By adding specific suffixes and prefixes, its application shifts from a simple direct blow to causative actions or intensive impacts.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative marker nic added to the tenth gaṇa root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to strike or to instigate a collision
scenarios.example_english: The enemy causes the soldier to strike.

meanings.English: To divide, to partition, to distribute

pedagogy.concept: The root vawa primarily means to divide or distribute. When modified into different derived forms, such as the causative, it indicates making someone else perform the act of division.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Adding the causative suffix ṇic to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to divide or distribute
scenarios.example_english: The father causes the wealth to be divided among the sons.

meanings.English: To cut, to sever, to split

pedagogy.concept: The root Cuwa~ primarily means to cut or sever. In its causative form, it indicates the action of causing something or someone to cut.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Adding the causative suffix -aya to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to cut or to make someone cut
scenarios.example_english: The man causes the tree to be cut.

meanings.English: To shine, to make clear, to manifest
meanings.Chinese: Fa guang, xian shi, zhao ming

pedagogy.concept: The root laja means to shine or make manifest. As a 10th-class curādi root, it inherently conveys a causative or effective sense of bringing something into light or display.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: 10th gaṇa present tense active third-person singular
scenarios.meaning: He or she illuminates or displays something
scenarios.example_english: The moon illuminates the night.

meanings.English: To shine, to make clear, to illuminate, to display

pedagogy.concept: The root vawi~ belongs to the tenth conjugation (curādis) and primarily means to make manifest or to cause to shine. In its causative-like tenth class form, it regularly takes the suffix -aya to indicate bringing something into light or making it visible.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, third person singular in the tenth gaṇa
scenarios.meaning: He/she/it illuminates or makes manifest
scenarios.example_english: The moon illuminates the night.

meanings.English: To manifest, to reveal, to shine, to display

pedagogy.concept: The root laji~ belongs to the tenth gaṇa and primarily denotes the action of making something manifest or bringing it to light. In its causative and derived nominal forms, this sense shifts towards actively causing manifestation or displaying an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat), third person singular of the tenth gaṇa (curādi-gaṇa)
scenarios.meaning: He reveals, causes to appear, or makes manifest.
scenarios.example_english: The leader reveals the truth.

meanings.English: To mix, to blend, to combine, to unite

pedagogy.concept: The root miSra in the tenth conjugation expresses the action of mixing or combining items. In its causative and derived forms, it emphasizes the intentional act of blending different substances or bringing separate entities together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, 3rd person singular, parasmaipada of the 10th conjugation curādi-gaṇa
scenarios.meaning: He mixes or blends
scenarios.example_english: The cook mixes water with milk.

meanings.English: To fight, to wage war, to battle

pedagogy.concept: The root sangrAma is a denominative or compound-derived verbal base meaning to fight or wage war. It generally takes parasmaipada endings.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat-lakāra), third person singular, parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: He fights or wages war.
scenarios.example_english: The hero fights the enemies.

meanings.English: To praise, to extol, to flatter
meanings.Hindi: praśansā karanā, stuti karanā, tarīpha karanā

pedagogy.concept: The root stoma belongs to the tenth gaṇa and carries the core sense of praise or flattery. In its standard causative or derived nominal forms, the focus shifts towards the act of eulogizing or composing hymns of praise.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, third-person singular, parasmaipada of the tenth gaṇa root
scenarios.meaning: He praises or flatters
scenarios.example_english: He praises the king.

meanings.English: To pierce the ear, to bore, to make a hole
meanings.German: das Ohr durchbohren, ein Loch machen

pedagogy.concept: The root Cidra in the tenth gaṇa specifically conveys the action of piercing or boring, commonly associated with piercing the earlobe for ornaments. When modified into causative or passive forms, the focus shifts to causing another agent to perform the piercing or the ear being pierced.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, third-person singular active form in the tenth gaṇa.
scenarios.meaning: He pierces or bores.
scenarios.example_english: The goldsmith pierces the ear.

meanings.English: To pierce, to bore, to split

pedagogy.concept: The root karṇa in the curādi gaṇa (class 10) primarily expresses the action of piercing, splitting, or boring. When formed into a causative or denominative-like verbal stem in class 10, the base meaning highlights the intentional act of making a hole or dividing an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (laṭ), third person singular, parasmaipada of class 10
scenarios.meaning: To pierce or to bore
scenarios.example_english: The artisan bores a hole in the wood.

meanings.English: To blind, to cause blindness, to obscure vision
meanings.Hindi: andha karna, drishti nasht karna, andhkara karna
meanings.Bengali: andho kara, drishti noshto kara, andhokar kora
meanings.French: aveugler, obscurcir la vue, priver de la vue
meanings.Chinese: shi mang, zhezhu shixian, qingchu shili

pedagogy.concept: The root anDa belongs to the cur-ādi gaṇa (class 10) and primarily conveys the sense of causing blindness or impairing vision. Through causative formations and derived nominals, it describes both physical blinding and metaphorical obscuration of clarity.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (laT) active voice of the cur-ādi gaṇa root.
scenarios.meaning: To blind or to obscure vision.
scenarios.example_english: He blinds the enemy with brilliance.

meanings.English: To punish, to fine, to chastise, to penalize
meanings.Hindi: Dand dena, saja dena, dandan karna

pedagogy.concept: The root danqa primarily means to punish or levy a fine. When modified into the causative or passive forms, it shifts the focus onto the agent causing the punishment or the subject undergoing the penalty.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Adding the nic suffix to engage another person in the act of punishing.
scenarios.meaning: To cause someone to punish or to order a punishment
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the thief to be punished.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Changing the verb voice to passive, making the recipient of the punishment the grammatical subject.
scenarios.meaning: To be punished or to suffer a fine
scenarios.example_english: The thief is punished by the king.

meanings.English: To mark, to brand, to characterize, to trace
meanings.Hindi: chinhit karna, lakshan dena, ankit karna
meanings.Bengali: chihniyta kora, lakshan deoa, ankito kora
meanings.Chinese: biao ji, biao shi, hua zhi

pedagogy.concept: The root anka in the tenth conjugation expresses the action of marking, stamping, or setting a characteristic sign. In its standard causative or derived verbal forms, it often emphasizes the act of stamping an emblem or clearly distinguishing something through a visible sign.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat), third person singular, parasmaipada of the tenth conjugation curadigana
scenarios.meaning: He marks, he brands, or he sets a sign upon something.
scenarios.example_english: The artisan marks the gold.

meanings.English: To mark, to characterize, to indicate

pedagogy.concept: The root anga in the tenth conjugation expresses the action of marking, designating, or indicating a characteristic. Through derivation into the causative or other forms, its basic notion of marking or pointing out can be directed towards objects or actions.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present indicative active, 3rd person singular in the tenth conjugation
scenarios.meaning: Marks or characterizes
scenarios.example_english: The artisan marks the statue.

meanings.English: To make happy, to give pleasure, to delight
meanings.Hindi: khush karna, anand dena, prasanna karna
meanings.French: rendre heureux, réjouir, donner du plaisir
meanings.Chinese: shi kuai le, zhu fu, shi man yi

pedagogy.concept: The root suKa in the tenth gaṇa expresses the action of making someone happy or causing pleasure. Through grammatical derivations, it can shift to describe a state of experiencing that happiness or expressing delight.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Denominative suffix ya applied to the derived nominal base to indicate causing happiness
scenarios.meaning: To cause happiness or comfort to someone
scenarios.example_english: He makes his friend happy.

meanings.English: (uncertain)

pedagogy.concept: This root relates to causing or experiencing distress or pain in the context of specific actions, but it has very limited productive usage and lacks standard comparative paradigms worth dividing into multiple scenarios.

meanings.English: To taste, to relish, to moisten, to lubricate
meanings.Kannada: Ruchi nodu, svadishtu padu, sneha madu, jneha
meanings.Hindi: Svad lena, ras chakhna, chikna karna
meanings.Bengali: Rasa nova, asvadana kara, snigdha kara

pedagogy.concept: The root rasa primarily means to taste or relish, and also to moisten or lubricate. Through causative and derivative formations, the sense shifts between experiencing a flavor or essence and imparting moisture or oiliness.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix -aya added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to taste or to flavor
scenarios.example_english: The cook flavors the food.

meanings.English: To spend, to expend, to disburse, to waste
meanings.Chinese: hua fei, kai xiao, xiao hao

pedagogy.concept: The root vyaya belongs to the tenth conjugation and primarily expresses the act of spending or expending wealth. Through causative and nominal derivations, it can highlight the action of causing expense or the state of being diminished.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense active (parasmaipada) of the primitive root in class 10.
scenarios.meaning: To spend money or wealth.
scenarios.example_english: He spends wealth.

meanings.English: To shape, to form, to give form
meanings.Hindi: Rup dena, akriti banana, srijan karna
meanings.Bengali: Rup dewa, gathan kara, akriti dewa

pedagogy.concept: The root rUp in the tenth gaNa primarily denotes the action of shaping, forming, or giving visual manifestation to something. Through the causative-like inflection of the curAdi gaNa, it expresses the active process of crafting or fashioning an object into a specific shape.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present indicative (laT) third person singular in the tenth gaNa (curAdi)
scenarios.meaning: To shape, to form, or to give a definite appearance to an object
scenarios.example_english: The sculptor shapes the stone

meanings.English: To divide, to split, to cut in two

pedagogy.concept: The root Ceda in the tenth gaṇa primarily expresses the action of dividing, cutting, or splitting something into two parts. In its causative and derived forms, the sense of active splitting or causing a division becomes more intensive.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: 10th gaṇa present tense third person singular
scenarios.meaning: Causes to cut or divide
scenarios.example_english: The carpenter causes the wood to be cut.

meanings.English: To cover, to conceal, to hide

pedagogy.concept: The root cada carries the primary sense of covering or concealing. In the causative form, it often denotes the act of causing to cover or displaying a false appearance, mimicking or pretending.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to form the causative stem chadayati, meaning to cause to cover or to disguise.
scenarios.meaning: To disguise, to pretend, or to put on a false appearance.
scenarios.example_english: He disguises his strength.

meanings.English: To urge, to impel, to incite, to direct

pedagogy.concept: The root lABa in the tenth gaṇa carries the causative sense of urging or directing someone to action. Through the addition of verbal prefixes or nominal suffixes, the fundamental nuance of impelling shifts toward specific directions or goals.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the prefix pra- to the tenth gaṇa present stem
scenarios.meaning: To strongly urge or incite someone toward an action
scenarios.example_english: The teacher strongly urges the student toward a good deed

meanings.English: To crush limbs, to bruise, to wound, to grind
meanings.Telugu: gatra vicurnana, gayamu ceyu, picci ceyu
meanings.Hindi: ang vicurna karna, ghayal karna, kuchalna
meanings.Bengali: anga vicurna kara, ahata kara, curna kara

pedagogy.concept: The root vraRa primarily means to crush or bruise the body. Through the causative form, it describes the action of causing someone to bruise or injure another.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to form the causative stem
scenarios.meaning: To cause to crush or to inflict a wound on another
scenarios.example_english: The army causes the enemy to be wounded.

meanings.English: To describe, to paint, to elaborate, to praise
meanings.Hindi: varnan karna, vyakhya karna, stuti karna
meanings.Bengali: varnana kara, byakhya kara, prashamsa kara

pedagogy.concept: The root varRa primarily conveys the act of describing, detailing, or attributing qualities to something. Through causative formations, it expresses the action of causing something to be described or depicted vividly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the root with the prefix vi
scenarios.meaning: To explain in detail or elaborate clearly
scenarios.example_english: The teacher explains the meaning of the text in detail.

meanings.English: To be green, to become green, to flourish

pedagogy.concept: The root parRa belongs to the tenth conjugation and primarily denotes the state of being green or flourishing. When used in causative or derivative forms, it shifts from merely describing a state of color to actively causing vegetation to become green.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, third-person singular in the active voice (parasmaipada)
scenarios.meaning: It turns green or flourishes
scenarios.example_english: In the spring, the earth turns green.

meanings.English: To see, to look, to observe, to perceive
meanings.Hindi: Dekhna, dekh bhal karna, avalokan karna

pedagogy.concept: The root vizka belongs to the tudadi or curadi classes in various contexts with the basic sense of seeing or observing. When used in different derived forms such as the causative, the sense shifts towards causing someone to see or display something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: curadi gaṇa present tense third person singular
scenarios.meaning: To show or to cause to see
scenarios.example_english: The teacher shows the picture to the student.

meanings.English: To throw, to cast, to hurl, to send

pedagogy.concept: The root kzip primarily means to throw or cast. When modified into the causative form, it emphasizes the action of impelling, inciting, or directing someone or something toward an action.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Adding the ṇic suffix to form kṣipayati
scenarios.meaning: To cause to throw, to impel, or to urge on
scenarios.example_english: The master urges the servant to drive the horse.

meanings.English: To dwell, to reside, to inhabit, to live

pedagogy.concept: The root vasa in the tenth gaṇa generally expresses dwelling or inhabiting. With various prefixes, it can nuance the sense to entering a dwelling, lingering, or dwelling together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the prefix ni- to the root vasa in the present tense
scenarios.meaning: To dwell, to reside in a place
scenarios.example_english: He dwells in the forest.

meanings.English: To cover, to conceal, to veil, to protect

pedagogy.concept: The root tutTa primarily means to cover or conceal. In its causative and derived nominal contexts, this sense shifts towards causing something to be covered or protected by an agent.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the causative suffixaya
scenarios.meaning: To cause to cover or to have something concealed
scenarios.example_english: The protector causes the house to be covered.

meanings.English: To cut, to sow, to reap, to scatter

pedagogy.concept: The root palyUla primarily combines the physical actions of cutting or reaping with scattering or sowing seeds. In its causative and derived nominal forms, the focus shifts between the agricultural act of harvesting and the dispersal of materials.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat), parasmaipada, third person singular
scenarios.meaning: He cuts or sows
scenarios.example_english: The farmer sows the seed in the field.

meanings.English: To speak, to converse, to talk
meanings.Chinese: shuo hua, jiang hua, tan hua

pedagogy.concept: The root ruṭh carries the core sense of speaking or language use. When modified into causative or derivative forms, the emphasis shifts toward causing speech or engaging in specific conversational contexts.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the tenth conjugation root
scenarios.meaning: To cause someone to speak or to make articulate sounds
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the student speak.

meanings.English: To see, to look at, to perceive

pedagogy.concept: The root Deka means to see or perceive. In its causative form, it typically indicates causing someone to see or showing something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to form the causative stem
scenarios.meaning: To cause to see, to show
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the student to see the book.
